headline: Peanut bunker floods Ram Island rocks, stripers on the seams, Race still waiting on albies
subhead: Stripers are working the boulder fields on peanut bunker and silversides while the fleet keeps one eye on the Race for the first bonito push.
body_markdown:
The bait is stacking on the rocks before anything else happens, and that's the tell worth watching this week. Peanut bunker and silversides are pouring over the boulder fields between Ram Island and Wamphassuc Point, pushed tight to the structure by the building current as the moon works toward full. When you see bait pinned against granite like that, holding in the eddies behind the humps instead of running open water, something's about to commit to it. Right now that something is striped bass — schoolie to mid-twenties mostly, with a few better fish mixed in on the last of the ebb — but the water's telling the fleet a second story is coming too.

New London is reading around 69.4 degrees, still comfortable, not the trigger-cold that pushes bait into panic. But the Race stays several degrees cooler than the Sound proper because of the tidal mixing through there, and that's exactly why it's the first place anyone with a fly rod or a spinning outfit loaded with small metal should be checking daily right now. We flagged this last week — said the Race was the logical landing spot for the bonito push building at Block Island and Point Judith, given the cold, current-scrubbed water it runs — and the pattern hasn't changed. Bonito are stacked to our east in numbers. False albacore are showing in Nantucket Sound on tiny bait, finicky but present. Neither has committed to Fishers Island Sound yet, but the ingredients are lining up, and this is a check-daily window through Labor Day.

Striped bass are the honest bite right now, and it's a structure game more than a blitz. The boulder fields off Ram Island and the rock piles tight to Wamphassuc Point are holding fish on the last two hours of the outgoing, when the current pulls bait off the shallows and funnels it through the guts between the rocks. Work those seams with a 3/4-ounce white or olive bucktail, short hops just off bottom, four to eight feet of water, and expect the takes right where the current breaks around a submerged boulder. Fly guys working the same water at first light with a sinking Clouser or a small white Deceiver are finding fish holding in the shadow lines off the ledge at Esker Point, especially on the slack before the tide turns. Nothing about this bite is fast — it's a fish here, a fish there, working through likely water and letting the structure do the sorting. But the sizes have been respectable, and a few fish pushing into the high twenties have come off the rocks on eels fished at dusk.

Today closes out the summer blackfish season in Connecticut waters, and a handful of boats worked the Stonington breakwater one more time on the last of the ebb, picking at tog in the four-to-six-pound range around the riprap on green crab. That fishery goes quiet now until the fall reopener, and the boulder fields that hold tog in October are the same rocks holding bass right now — worth remembering where you marked fish, because those same humps will be productive again once the season reopens.

Fluke have softened into the pattern you'd expect for the end of August — fair, not great, with fish sliding toward the deeper channel edges of Little Narragansett Bay and the cuts through Watch Hill Passage as the shallow water in the coves warms under the afternoon sun. This tracks with what we said last week — a normal seasonal shuffle, not a fluke collapse. Gulp and bucktail combos, white or pink, worked slow along the channel drop-offs on the last of the incoming, are still putting keeper-class fish in the boat, just not in the numbers you'd see in July. Black sea bass remain a dependable structure fish through this stretch — the rock piles and mussel beds off Fishers Island are holding them, and they'll stay a steady producer as the water cools into fall.

The next few days set up around the building moon and the tide swings that come with it. More tidal flow means more bait getting pushed and concentrated against structure, which is exactly the mechanism that turns a scattered striper bite into something closer to a real push. If the wind stays out of the south and southwest through the weekend, keep working the boulder fields on the outgoing and watch the Race every day for the first bonito or albie sign — small profile epoxy jigs and 00 Deceivers in the boat bag now, because when that push arrives here it tends to arrive fast, and the guys ready for it are the ones who get the first week of it. Labor Day traffic will be heavier on the water, so first light and the two hours around the tide change are worth prioritizing before the pressure builds. If there's only one window to fish this week, work the last of the ebb around Ram Island or Wamphassuc at daybreak — that's where the bait's been thickest and the bass have been most willing to show themselves.
